title: k-means against the clock
objectives: Write k-means with a fixed start, an empty-cluster rule and a stopping test inside fifteen minutes.

screens.title: Assign by hand
screens.prose: This lesson takes about fifteen minutes; the drill after it has a pace of fifteen minutes. You met k-means in `stat-learning` l16. Six points, $k = 2$, and the fixed start: the first two points, $(0, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$, are the centres.
screens.question: Give each point the index of its nearest starting centre, 0 or 1.

hints.text: Compare squared distances to $(0, 0)$ and to $(0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: $0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1$: the far points all join centre 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute both squared distances for each point.

explain.text: Centre $(0, 1)$ is one unit nearer the far group, so all three far points join it. A poor start like this is why the passes matter.

canvas.caption: pass 1: assigned to the starting centres

screens.title: Assign, update, repeat
screens.prose: Step through the passes. Assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to its points' mean, and stop when no label changes.

frames.caption: pass 1: assigned to the starting centres
update 1: centres move to their means

screens.question: How many assignment passes run before the algorithm stops, counting the one that changes nothing?

hints.text: Count the frames that say "pass".
Pass 3 changes no label.
Three passes, two updates.

feedback.correct: Three passes: the third confirms nothing changed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count assignment passes, including the last.

byKey.updates: That counts the centre updates. The stopping test needs one more assignment pass.

explain.text: Three passes: the algorithm only knows it has converged after a pass that changes no label. So the passes always number one more than the useful updates.

screens.title: The first update

state.caption: pass 1: assigned to the starting centres

screens.question: What is the $y$-coordinate of cluster 1's new centre?

hints.text: Average the four $y$-coordinates.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the $y$-coordinates of the four points.

byKey.three: You left out $(0, 1)$, which is still in cluster 1 after pass 1.

explain.text: The centre is $(20/4, 17/4) = (4, 4.25)$. The stray point $(0, 1)$ drags it towards the origin, and on pass 2 that point leaves.

canvas.caption: update 1: centres move to their means

screens.title: Where it ends
screens.prose: After pass 2 the clusters are the three near points and the three far points. The centres become $(1/3, 1/3)$ and $(16/3, 16/3)$.
screens.question: What is the inertia, the total squared distance from each point to its centre? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Each cluster is three points around its mean.
For the near cluster: $\tfrac{2}{9} + \tfrac{5}{9} + \tfrac{5}{9} = \tfrac{4}{3}$.
The far cluster is the same shape: $\tfrac{4}{3} + \tfrac{4}{3} = \tfrac{8}{3}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the squared distances in both clusters.

byKey.one: That is one cluster. The far cluster adds the same again.
byKey.root: You added distances, not squared distances.

explain.text: The two clusters are copies of one shape, each with squared distances $\tfrac{2}{9}$, $\tfrac{5}{9}$ and $\tfrac{5}{9}$. The total is $\tfrac{8}{3} = 2.6667$.

screens.title: When to stop
screens.prose: A candidate says: "I stop when the inertia looks flat, say a change under 1%."
screens.question: What is the problem?

options.text: A flat inertia can hide labels that still change; stop when no label changes.
Nothing: inertia can only fall, so a flat inertia is convergence.
options.why: It never rises, but a small fall can still come with a label change. Labels are exact.

options.text: It is too slow; use a fixed 10 passes.
options.why: A fixed count can stop early on a slow case or waste passes on a fast one.

options.text: Inertia can rise, so it may never look flat.
options.why: With exact means and nearest assignment, inertia never rises.

hints.text: What is the exact sign that nothing will change again?
If no label changes, the centres stay put, and so does everything after.
Labels give an exact test; a tolerance on inertia does not.

feedback.correct: Stop on unchanged labels: exact and cheap.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which quantity can be compared exactly?

byKey.fine: A 1% change can still move a point; only unchanged labels guarantee a fixed point.

explain.text: Unchanged labels mean unchanged centres, so every later pass is identical: an exact fixed point. A tolerance on inertia is a guess, and an interviewer will ask what tolerance.

screens.title: An empty cluster
screens.prose: Points $(0, 0)$, $(0, 0)$, $(5, 5)$ with $k = 2$: both starting centres are $(0, 0)$. Ties go to the lower index.
screens.question: What happens to cluster 1 on pass 1, and what should the code do?

options.text: It gets no points; keep its old centre, as the rule you stated says.
Its mean is the mean of nothing; let it be nan.
options.why: A nan centre poisons every later distance. State a rule instead.

options.text: Delete it and carry on with one cluster.
options.why: Then the function returns fewer than $k$ centres, breaking its contract.

options.text: Move it to a random point.
options.why: Possible, but it makes the result depend on a random stream; with a fixed start, keep the centre.

hints.text: Every point ties between two equal centres.
Ties go to centre 0, so centre 1 has no points.
The mean of no points is undefined: keep the old centre.

feedback.correct: Keep it, and say the rule before you code.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The mean of no points needs a rule.

byKey.nan: A nan centre makes every later distance nan.

explain.text: Say the empty-cluster rule and the tie rule before writing code. Here centre 1 stays at $(0, 0)$, wins the two $(0, 0)$ points on pass 2, and the run ends with centres $(5, 5)$ and $(0, 0)$.

screens.title: Better starts, in one sentence each
screens.prose: The interview asked for a fixed start, so the result is reproducible. Say the alternatives from `stat-learning` l16 in one sentence each. k-means++ picks each new centre with probability proportional to $D(x)^2$, the squared distance to the nearest chosen centre. Several starts keep the run with the lowest inertia, $$\sum_i \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{c_i}\|^2.$$
screens.question: Why does k-means++ help?

options.text: It spreads the starting centres out, so poor starts like ours are rare.
It guarantees the global minimum of the inertia.
options.why: It gives a start whose expected inertia is within a log factor of the best, not the best itself.
Passes cost the same; it needs fewer of them and lands lower.

feedback.correct: Spread-out starts avoid two centres in one group.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about our start: two centres in the same group.

explain.text: Our start put both centres in one group, which cost an extra pass. k-means++ makes that unlikely by favouring far points.

screens.title: Clustering stocks
screens.prose: A fund clusters stocks by their last 250 daily returns, each series standardised to mean 0 and sd 1. For such series, $\|\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}\|^2 = 2T(1 - \rho)$.
screens.question: Two stocks have correlation 0.6. What is their squared distance?

hints.text: Use $2T(1 - \rho)$ with $T = 250$.

explain.text: For standardised series the squared distance is $2T(1 - \rho) = 200$. So k-means on standardised returns groups stocks by correlation, which is what the desk wants.

mutants.symptom: Takes the minimum over points instead of centres.
Breaks ties towards the higher index.
Uses the city-block distance instead of the Euclidean one.

byKey.test-1: The six points come out wrong. Build an $(n, k)$ table and take the minimum along `axis=1`, over centres.
byKey.test-2: A tie went to the higher index. `argmin` returns the first minimum, which is the lower index.

screens.title: Update in code
screens.prose: Write `update_centres(points, labels, old)`: each centre becomes the mean of its points; a cluster with no points keeps its `old` centre. Do not change `old`.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np


def update_centres(points, labels, old):
    # the mean of each cluster's points; an empty cluster keeps its old centre
    ...
widget.how: Submit runs 5 hidden tests: the first update of this lesson's six points, an empty cluster, $k = 1$, the old centres, a float array, left unchanged, and one dimension with an empty cluster 0. Numbers are compared to $10^{-9}$.

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def update_centres(points, labels, old):
    P = np.asarray(points, dtype=float)
    new = np.array(old, dtype=float)
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    for j in range(len(new)):
        new[j] = P[labels == j].mean(axis=0)
    return new
mutants.symptom: Takes the mean of an empty cluster, which is nan.
Sums the cluster instead of averaging it.
Starts from zeros, so an empty cluster moves to the origin.
Wraps the caller's float array without copying it, so the update overwrites the old centres.

hints.text: Start from a copy of `old`.
Loop over the $k$ clusters.
Replace a row only when the cluster has at least one point.

feedback.correct: Means where there are points, the old centre where there are none.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Average each cluster and handle the empty one.

byKey.test-1: The first update is off: cluster 1 should be $(4, 4.25)$. Average the points, do not sum them.
byKey.test-2: The empty cluster came out as nan. Replace a centre only when its cluster has points.
byKey.test-5: Empty cluster 0 should keep its old centre, 1. Start from a copy of `old`, not from zeros.
byKey.test-4: Your update overwrote the caller's centres. Copy with `np.array(old, dtype=float)`, not `np.asarray`.

explain.text: Copying `old` first makes the empty-cluster rule free: a cluster with no points is simply never overwritten.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer goes on: "Vectorise the assignment, and tell me what it costs." Then sit the drill `#drill/mi-kmeans-fixed-start` (pace 15 minutes).
screens.question: What is the memory cost of the broadcast distance table for $n$ points, $k$ centres, $d$ features?

options.text: $n \times k \times d$ for the differences, before the sum.
Only $n \times d$, the size of the points.
options.why: Broadcasting builds every point-centre difference, which is $k$ times larger.

options.text: Only $k \times d$, the size of the centres.
options.why: Every point is compared with every centre, so $n$ enters too.

hints.text: The broadcast forms $\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j$ for every pair.
Each difference has $d$ entries.
That is $nkd$ numbers before summing over $d$.

feedback.correct: $nkd$ for the differences; use $\|x\|^2 - 2x\cdot\mu + \|\mu\|^2$ to need only $nk$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the point-centre differences.

byKey.nd: The broadcast compares every point with every centre.

explain.text: For a million points and 100 centres in 50 dimensions the difference array holds $5 \times 10^9$ numbers. Expanding the square needs only the $n \times k$ table, from one matrix product.

ideas: Before coding, state the start rule, the tie rule, the empty-cluster rule and the stopping test.
Stop when no label changes: the six points converge after three passes to $(1/3, 1/3)$ and $(16/3, 16/3)$, inertia $8/3$.
An empty cluster keeps its old centre; vectorise the assignment with one broadcast, costing $nkd$.
summary.trap: Stopping when the inertia looks flat can stop while labels still change; stop on unchanged labels.

quiz.question: A cluster holds $(2, 3)$, $(4, 1)$ and $(6, 8)$. What is the $y$-coordinate of its centre?

byKey.median: That is the median. k-means uses the mean.

explain.text: The centre is the mean, $(12/3, 12/3) = (4, 4)$, so its $y$-coordinate is 4.

quiz.question: A point is exactly as far from centre 0 as from centre 2. With the stated rule, which label does it get?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ties go to the lower index.

byKey.high: The rule sends ties to the lower index.

explain.text: The rule was ties to the lower index, which is what `argmin` does. Saying it aloud makes the output reproducible.

quiz.question: Labels did not change on pass 7. Which is true?

options.text: The centres will never change again.
Run a few more passes to be sure.
options.why: With the same labels the means are the same, so every later pass repeats this one.

options.text: The inertia is at its global minimum.
options.why: Converged means a fixed point of this start; another start can do better.

feedback.correct: A fixed point of the algorithm.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What do unchanged labels do to the centres?

explain.text: Same labels give the same means, so the state repeats for ever. It is a local fixed point; the global minimum is another matter.
